answer.generated: Mutual exclusion and deadlock are two critical issues that arise when multiple concurrent processes attempt to access shared resources. Mutual exclusion ensures that only one process can operate on a resource at any given time, preventing race conditions and inconsistent states. Deadlock occurs when two or more processes hold resources while waiting for others, creating a circular wait that halts progress. Both problems must be addressed simultaneously because a solution to one often exacerbates the other. For example, overly aggressive locking can prevent deadlock but introduce starvation, while lax locks may cause deadlock yet improve throughput. Thus, an operating system must balance mutual exclusion policies with deadlock prevention strategies to ensure reliable concurrent execution.
